p1-c0-b0.label: Productivity gap honestly diagnosed
p1-c0-b0.detailText: The gap itself is thoroughly and repeatedly documented — the OECD's 2026 survey finds output per capita persistently below the top half of the OECD with convergence stalled. Marked down because the dedicated institution for diagnosing it, the Productivity Commission, was disestablished in February 2024. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/04/foundations-for-growth-and-competitiveness-2026_f68a156b/full-report/new-zealand_c6b7a0e7.html

p1-c0-b1.label: Diffuse policy response acknowledged
p1-c0-b1.detailText: Government and officials acknowledge weak productivity, and the OECD notes broad reforms are starting to address its roots. What is far less acknowledged is the specific charge in the article — that the response is diffuse rather than focused. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/economic-surveys/new-zealand-economic-snapshot.html

p1-c0-b2.label: Comparator country lessons drawn
p1-c0-b2.detailText: Comparator economies are cited frequently in New Zealand debate, but citation is not the same as systematically drawing and applying the policy lessons. This is the article's central complaint and the assessment reflects it. Evidence: https://nzmanufacturer.co.nz/2026/08/new-zealands-favourite-economies-do-not-succeed-by-accident/

p1-c0-b3.label: Implicit industrial policy recognised
p1-c0-b3.detailText: New Zealand already runs de facto industrial policy — an R&D tax incentive, the uncapped Investment Boost, fast-track approvals, a defence industrial strategy — but rarely names it as such, so the 'neutrality' framing survives largely unchallenged. Evidence: https://budget.govt.nz/budget/pdfs/releases/l25a-factsheet-investment-boost.pdf

p1-c0-b4.label: Narrow export base risk understood
p1-c0-b4.detailText: Well understood and formally analysed: Treasury has measured rising export concentration, and dairy's dominance is tracked in every SOPI release. Understanding is strong; response is not. Evidence: https://www.treasury.govt.nz/publications/research-and-commentary/rangitaki-blog/mei-special-topic-new-zealands-increasing-export-concentration

p1-c1-b0.label: Picking-winners debate reframed
p1-c1-b0.detailText: The picking-winners objection remains the default position rather than a settled debate. The clearest signal is the closure of the Industry Transformation Plan programme, which was the main sector-specific vehicle. Evidence: https://www.mbie.govt.nz/business-and-employment/economic-growth/previous-economic-development-work/industry-transformation-plans/advanced-manufacturing

p1-c1-b1.label: Safeguards against propping weak firms agreed
p1-c1-b1.detailText: No explicit framework exists for stopping support propping up weak firms. Because most support is broad and untargeted rather than selective, the risk is lower — but that is an accident of design, not a safeguard. Evidence: https://budget.govt.nz/budget/pdfs/releases/l25a-factsheet-investment-boost.pdf

p1-c1-b2.label: Cross-party durability sought
p1-c1-b2.detailText: The record is one of reversal: Industry Transformation Plans closed, Te Pūkenga disestablished, the Productivity Commission repealed, resource management law rewritten twice. The National Infrastructure Plan, where the Government accepted all sixteen recommendations and sought cross-party engagement, is the notable exception. Evidence: https://www.treasury.govt.nz/publications/infrastructure-plan/government-response-national-infrastructure-plan-2026

p1-c2-b0.label: Focused industrial policy adopted
p1-c2-b0.detailText: New Zealand has no focused industrial policy. The Industry Transformation Plan programme, the closest thing to one, has been closed. Evidence: https://www.mbie.govt.nz/business-and-employment/economic-growth/previous-economic-development-work/industry-transformation-plans/advanced-manufacturing

p1-c2-b1.label: Priority sectors selected transparently
p1-c2-b1.detailText: There is no current transparent mechanism for selecting priority sectors. The ITP programme performed this function and was discontinued. Evidence: https://www.mbie.govt.nz/business-and-employment/economic-growth/previous-economic-development-work/industry-transformation-plans/advanced-manufacturing

p1-c2-b2.label: Long-term funding commitment made
p1-c2-b2.detailText: Investment Boost is a genuinely large commitment at roughly $1.7 billion a year, but it is a broad capital subsidy rather than a long-term industrial commitment, and reported policy flip-flopping undercuts its planning value. Evidence: https://budget.govt.nz/budget/pdfs/releases/l25a-factsheet-investment-boost.pdf

p1-c3-b0.label: Stable long-term direction sustained
p1-c3-b0.detailText: Direction has not been stable across electoral cycles in vocational education, science, productivity institutions or resource management. Infrastructure is the one area where a genuinely long-horizon plan now exists. Evidence: https://www.treasury.govt.nz/publications/infrastructure-plan/government-response-national-infrastructure-plan-2026

p1-c3-b1.label: Policy credibility with firms established
p1-c3-b1.detailText: Firms face a planning environment where major settings change between governments. Credibility is the casualty, and it is the hardest thing on this page to rebuild. Evidence: https://www.treasury.govt.nz/publications/infrastructure-plan/government-response-national-infrastructure-plan-2026

p2-c0-b0.label: Advanced manufacturing skill needs identified
p2-c0-b0.detailText: Industry Skills Boards, operating from January 2026 with majority industry governance, are designed precisely to identify sector skill needs. The mechanism is sound but brand new and unproven. Evidence: https://www.education.govt.nz/our-work/strategies-policies-and-programmes/tertiary-and-further-education/redesign-vocational-education-and-training-system

p2-c0-b1.label: Employer demand signals collected
p2-c0-b1.detailText: Majority industry governance of the new standard-setting bodies is a real structural improvement in how employer demand reaches the training system. Evidence: https://www.education.govt.nz/our-work/strategies-policies-and-programmes/tertiary-and-further-education/redesign-vocational-education-and-training-system

p2-c1-b0.label: Vocational provision aligned to industry
p2-c1-b0.detailText: Alignment to industry is the stated purpose of the 2026 reform, but the system is mid-transition and the Ministry's own advice differed from the Minister's on core design decisions. Evidence: https://www.education.govt.nz/our-work/strategies-policies-and-programmes/tertiary-and-further-education/redesign-vocational-education-and-training-system

p2-c1-b1.label: Engineering and technician places expanded
p2-c1-b1.detailText: No evidence of expanded engineering or technician provision. Polytechnic financial difficulties, acknowledged as decades in the making, point the other way. Evidence: https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/delivering-our-promise-disestablish-te-p%C5%ABkenga

p2-c1-b2.label: Work-based learning strengthened
p2-c1-b2.detailText: Work-based learning is being moved twice in two years — into Industry Skills Boards, then out again to polytechnics, wānanga or private providers. Continuity is the risk. Evidence: https://www.tec.govt.nz/strategic-initiatives/vocational-education-system/changes-to-the-vocational-education-and-training-vet-system/new-work-based-learning-model

p2-c2-b0.label: Trainee and apprentice numbers lifted
p2-c2-b0.detailText: Around 250,000 people are in vocational education annually with roughly half training on the job, so the base is substantial. Whether numbers lift through the transition is untested. Evidence: https://www.education.govt.nz/our-work/strategies-policies-and-programmes/tertiary-and-further-education/redesign-vocational-education-and-training-system

p2-c2-b1.label: Specialist skills sourced through migration
p2-c2-b1.detailText: Skilled migration settings function reasonably well for scarce specialist roles, and this is one of the faster levers New Zealand actually has. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/economic-surveys/new-zealand-economic-snapshot.html

p2-c3-b0.label: Firms recruit needed technical skills
p2-c3-b0.detailText: Persistent labour shortages are cited as a driver of automation interest, which indicates firms are not readily recruiting the technical skills they need. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/economic-surveys/new-zealand-economic-snapshot.html

p2-c3-b1.label: Existing workforce reskilled for automation
p2-c3-b1.detailText: There is no substantial national programme for reskilling the existing workforce for automation, which is exactly the gap the article points to in comparator countries. Evidence: https://nzmanufacturer.co.nz/2026/08/new-zealands-favourite-economies-do-not-succeed-by-accident/

p2-c3-b2.label: Management and leadership capability lifted
p2-c3-b2.detailText: The OECD finds New Zealand SME owners have strong operational skills but significant gaps in financial and capital-structure capability, which constrains their ability to scale. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_27daa8d8/full-report/unlocking-capital-markets-to-drive-growth_d1f7a7f7.html

p2-c3-b3.label: Skilled staff retained in New Zealand
p2-c3-b3.detailText: Retention is structurally hard while output per capita and wages lag the countries competing for the same people. Convergence with the OECD top half has stalled. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/04/foundations-for-growth-and-competitiveness-2026_f68a156b/full-report/new-zealand_c6b7a0e7.html

p2-c4-b0.label: Commercially relevant skills base built
p2-c4-b0.detailText: The reform is aimed at commercial relevance and the governance change is real, but the outcome cannot yet be observed part-way through a two-year transition. Evidence: https://www.tec.govt.nz/strategic-initiatives/vocational-education-system/changes-to-the-vocational-education-and-training-vet-system/new-work-based-learning-model

p3-c0-b0.label: Low capital intensity diagnosed
p3-c0-b0.detailText: Explicitly and repeatedly diagnosed. The OECD's 2026 capital markets chapter names persistently low capital intensity as a direct contributor to the productivity gap. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_27daa8d8/full-report/unlocking-capital-markets-to-drive-growth_d1f7a7f7.html

p3-c0-b1.label: Small firm adoption barriers identified
p3-c0-b1.detailText: Barriers facing smaller firms are reasonably well identified, including financial capability gaps, and a government AI pilot for small businesses targets them directly. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_27daa8d8/full-report/unlocking-capital-markets-to-drive-growth_d1f7a7f7.html

p3-c0-b2.label: Weak business investment understood
p3-c0-b2.detailText: Well understood. The OECD finds labour utilisation strong but the investment rate low — the diagnosis is not in dispute. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/04/foundations-for-growth-and-competitiveness-2026_f68a156b/full-report/new-zealand_c6b7a0e7.html

p3-c1-b0.label: Advisory and diagnostic support available
p3-c1-b0.detailText: Support exists through the Regional Business Partner Network and NZTE readiness programmes, but the OECD describes current SME support as limited relative to the capability gap. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_27daa8d8/full-report/unlocking-capital-markets-to-drive-growth_d1f7a7f7.html

p3-c1-b1.label: Co-investment for automation offered
p3-c1-b1.detailText: Investment Boost is a broad tax deduction available to any business for almost any asset, not targeted automation co-investment. The $30 million of ITP actions that were sector-specific have ended. Evidence: https://www.mbie.govt.nz/business-and-employment/economic-growth/previous-economic-development-work/industry-transformation-plans/advanced-manufacturing

p3-c1-b2.label: Digital tools proven through demonstrators
p3-c1-b2.detailText: Demonstrator activity is thin. A small-business AI pilot is the main current example, well short of the shared demonstration infrastructure the article attributes to comparator economies. Evidence: https://nzmanufacturer.co.nz/2026/08/new-zealands-favourite-economies-do-not-succeed-by-accident/

p3-c2-b0.label: Firms invest in automation and digital tools
p3-c2-b0.detailText: Early Inland Revenue monitoring of Investment Boost finds firms adjusting timing and prioritisation, but concludes it will take time for effects to flow through, and that survey uptake is likely overstated. Evidence: https://www.taxpolicy.ird.govt.nz/-/media/project/ir/tp/publications/2026/analytical-note-investment-boost.pdf

p3-c2-b1.label: Process improvement capability embedded
p3-c2-b1.detailText: Process improvement capability is uneven across the sector and not systematically supported; no national programme addresses it directly. Evidence: https://www.mbie.govt.nz/business-and-employment/economic-growth/previous-economic-development-work/industry-transformation-plans/advanced-manufacturing

p3-c3-b0.label: Firm-level productivity lifted
p3-c3-b0.detailText: Recent movement is genuinely positive — manufacturing grew 1.9 percent in the March 2026 quarter and was the largest contributor to GDP growth. The long-run trend remains the problem. Evidence: https://stats.govt.nz/topics/manufacturing-and-production

p3-c3-b1.label: Higher-value work retained onshore
p3-c3-b1.detailText: The OECD warns of a markedly raised risk of rapid deindustrialisation, with high contract electricity prices forcing temporary and permanent industrial shutdowns. Value is moving offshore, not being retained. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_3ec5de98-en/full-report/towards-a-more-affordable-secure-and-sustainable-electricity-system_8422a0e1.html

p4-c0-b0.label: Energy cost and reliability constraints mapped
p4-c0-b0.detailText: Exceptionally well mapped. The OECD devoted a survey chapter to it, PwC's 2026 gas study models supply and demand, and MBIE publishes quarterly price and consumption data. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_3ec5de98-en/full-report/towards-a-more-affordable-secure-and-sustainable-electricity-system_8422a0e1.html

p4-c0-b1.label: Industrial land shortages identified
p4-c0-b1.detailText: Industrial land supply is not tracked nationally with anything like the rigour applied to energy, so the constraint is understood locally and anecdotally rather than systematically. Evidence: https://www.treasury.govt.nz/publications/infrastructure-plan/government-response-national-infrastructure-plan-2026

p4-c0-b2.label: Consent processing delays quantified
p4-c0-b2.detailText: Quantified in concrete terms: the Infrastructure Commission found consenting delays put New Zealand on track to miss 11 to 15 percent of energy and transport emissions reductions by 2050. Evidence: https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/rma-reforms-deliver-jobs-and-growth

p4-c0-b3.label: Grid connection bottlenecks understood
p4-c0-b3.detailText: Connection and firming constraints are recognised — the OECD points to barriers to investment in non-gas firming capacity — but grid queue transparency is weaker than the price analysis. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_3ec5de98-en/full-report/towards-a-more-affordable-secure-and-sustainable-electricity-system_8422a0e1.html

p4-c1-b0.label: Affordable reliable industrial energy secured
p4-c1-b0.detailText: The clearest red on the board. The OECD finds wholesale and forward prices uncomfortably high internationally, far above Nordic countries with similarly renewables-dominated systems, with falling gas reserves compounding it. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_3ec5de98-en/full-report/towards-a-more-affordable-secure-and-sustainable-electricity-system_8422a0e1.html

p4-c1-b1.label: Serviced industrial land made available
p4-c1-b1.detailText: No national programme delivers serviced industrial land. It sits with councils and is shaped by a planning system currently mid-replacement. Evidence: https://www.bellgully.com/insights/resource-management-act-replacements-unveiled/

p4-c1-b2.label: Consent and connection timelines shortened
p4-c1-b2.detailText: Real movement: the Fast-track Approvals Act is operating and the Natural Environment and Planning Bills passed select committee in July 2026. But the new system is not in effect until 2027, so the gain is prospective. Evidence: https://www.bellgully.com/insights/resource-management-act-replacements-unveiled/

p4-c2-b0.label: Industrial projects proceed in New Zealand
p4-c2-b0.detailText: Mixed evidence pulling both ways — fast-track approval was granted for New Zealand's largest wind farm, while energy costs are forcing industrial closures elsewhere. Evidence: https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/rma-reforms-deliver-jobs-and-growth

p4-c2-b1.label: Expansion decisions kept onshore
p4-c2-b1.detailText: Major industrial users including Methanex and Ballance's Kapuni plant face closure or exit decisions, with PwC noting uncertainty over the future of several large users. Evidence: https://www.pwc.co.nz/pdfs/2026-pdfs/pwc-new-zealand-2026-gas-supply-and-demand-study.pdf

p5-c0-b0.label: Applied research priorities set with industry
p5-c0-b0.detailText: Business R&D reached $4.1 billion in 2025 but grew only 0.4 percent on 2024, suggesting priorities are not being reset with industry at any pace. Evidence: https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/research-and-development-survey-2025/

p5-c0-b1.label: Research centres focused on industry needs
p5-c0-b1.detailText: The research institute system has been under repeated restructuring, which makes sustained industry focus harder to establish than the structure itself implies. Evidence: https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/research-and-development-survey-2025/

p5-c1-b0.label: Firms connected to research providers
p5-c1-b0.detailText: Direct evidence of weak connection: analysis of business R&D finds only about 5 percent of business-funded R&D happens in the government sector and even less in higher education. Evidence: https://businessnz.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/240919-Support-for-business-RD.pdf

p5-c1-b1.label: Industry secondment and doctoral routes used
p5-c1-b1.detailText: Follows from the same finding — very little business R&D money flows into universities, which is where secondment and industry doctoral routes would show up. Evidence: https://businessnz.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/240919-Support-for-business-RD.pdf

p5-c1-b2.label: Shared testbeds and pilot lines available
p5-c1-b2.detailText: Shared testbeds and pilot lines were an explicit ITP action area, and that programme has closed without an evident successor. Evidence: https://www.mbie.govt.nz/business-and-employment/economic-growth/previous-economic-development-work/industry-transformation-plans/advanced-manufacturing

p5-c1-b3.label: Intellectual property terms made simpler
p5-c1-b3.detailText: Deliberately not assessed. Public evidence on whether intellectual property and contracting terms between firms and research providers have become simpler is not available at a national level, and a colour here would be a guess. Evidence: https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/research-and-development-survey-2025/

p5-c2-b0.label: Prototypes validated at production scale
p5-c2-b0.detailText: Some genuine capability exists in agritech, medtech and space, but validation at production scale is firm-by-firm rather than systematically supported. Evidence: https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/research-and-development-survey-2025/

p5-c2-b1.label: Commercialisation pathways navigated
p5-c2-b1.detailText: Business R&D is heavily concentrated in computer services and miscellaneous services; all manufacturing outside machinery and equipment accounts for roughly 9 percent. Commercialisation into physical products is thin. Evidence: https://businessnz.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/240919-Support-for-business-RD.pdf

p5-c2-b2.label: Clusters formed around real strengths
p5-c2-b2.detailText: Real clusters have formed in agritech, medtech and aerospace, but around firm-level success rather than deliberate cluster policy of the kind the article describes in Ireland. Evidence: https://nzmanufacturer.co.nz/2026/08/new-zealands-favourite-economies-do-not-succeed-by-accident/

p5-c3-b0.label: New high-value products launched
p5-c3-b0.detailText: New Zealand does launch genuinely high-value products, and total R&D expenditure has risen to $6.4 billion. Volume relative to the size of the economy remains the constraint. Evidence: https://www.stats.govt.nz/information-releases/research-and-development-survey-2025/

p5-c3-b1.label: Export revenue from local ideas grown
p5-c3-b1.detailText: Export revenue is growing strongly, but overwhelmingly from primary production rather than from commercialised local research — food and fibre alone is forecast at $64.3 billion. Evidence: https://www.mpi.govt.nz/resources-and-forms/economic-intelligence/situation-and-outlook-for-primary-industries

p5-c4-b0.label: Value from local research retained onshore
p5-c4-b0.detailText: The capital gap pushes companies offshore. The Elevate fund exists specifically because the Series A and B gap was leading innovative young companies to leave. Evidence: https://nzsuperfund.nz/how-we-invest/investing-in-nz/venture-capital/

p6-c0-b0.label: Scale-up gap identified beyond start-ups
p6-c0-b0.detailText: Precisely identified and acted on institutionally — the Elevate NZ Venture Fund was created specifically to address the Series A and B gap for companies past the start-up stage. Evidence: https://nzsuperfund.nz/how-we-invest/investing-in-nz/venture-capital/

p6-c0-b1.label: Growth capital gaps identified
p6-c0-b1.detailText: The OECD devoted an entire 2026 survey chapter to New Zealand's shallow capital markets and limited access to long-term domestic funding. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_27daa8d8/full-report/unlocking-capital-markets-to-drive-growth_d1f7a7f7.html

p6-c0-b2.label: Small firm scale constraints understood
p6-c0-b2.detailText: Well characterised: the OECD identifies SME gaps in capital structure and equity financing knowledge as a direct constraint on scaling. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_27daa8d8/full-report/unlocking-capital-markets-to-drive-growth_d1f7a7f7.html

p6-c1-b0.label: Growth and expansion capital available
p6-c1-b0.detailText: Improving but still shallow. New Zealand private capital funds raised roughly $1.9 billion across 2024 and 2025 and venture activity is rising, against an OECD finding of limited risk capital overall. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_27daa8d8/full-report/unlocking-capital-markets-to-drive-growth_d1f7a7f7.html

p6-c1-b1.label: Export credit and guarantees accessible
p6-c1-b1.detailText: Export credit facilities exist, but the OECD's diagnosis of limited long-term finance applies to exporters as much as to domestic firms. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_27daa8d8/full-report/unlocking-capital-markets-to-drive-growth_d1f7a7f7.html

p6-c2-b0.label: Management depth built in growing firms
p6-c2-b0.detailText: Management depth is a documented constraint — strong operational skills paired with weak financial and capital-structure capability is precisely what limits firms at the scaling point. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_27daa8d8/full-report/unlocking-capital-markets-to-drive-growth_d1f7a7f7.html

p6-c2-b1.label: Firms invest in productive assets
p6-c2-b1.detailText: Investment Boost is designed to shift exactly this, and early monitoring shows firms adjusting investment timing and prioritisation, but the effect on the capital stock is not yet observable. Evidence: https://www.taxpolicy.ird.govt.nz/-/media/project/ir/tp/publications/2026/analytical-note-investment-boost.pdf

p6-c2-b2.label: International standards and compliance met
p6-c2-b2.detailText: A relative strength. New Zealand exporters meet demanding traceability, food safety and provenance requirements in major markets as a matter of course. Evidence: https://www.mpi.govt.nz/resources-and-forms/economic-intelligence/situation-and-outlook-for-primary-industries

p6-c2-b3.label: Export market knowledge built
p6-c2-b3.detailText: NZTE provides market knowledge and readiness support, but the OECD still points to reduced foreign investment screening and faster technology adoption as unfinished work. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/economic-surveys/new-zealand-economic-snapshot.html

p6-c3-b0.label: Export markets entered and held
p6-c3-b0.detailText: Exports have been resilient and are supporting the current recovery, with food and fibre revenue forecast to rise 6 percent to a record $64.3 billion. Evidence: https://www.mpi.govt.nz/resources-and-forms/economic-intelligence/situation-and-outlook-for-primary-industries

p6-c3-b1.label: Places won in global supply chains
p6-c3-b1.detailText: Positions in global supply chains are real in some niches but limited outside primary products, and the OECD recommends reducing FDI screening restrictions to improve integration. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/economic-surveys/new-zealand-economic-snapshot.html

p6-c4-b0.label: More firms scaled beyond small size
p6-c4-b0.detailText: The scale-up problem persists — this is the gap Elevate was built to close, and shallow capital markets continue to constrain firm growth and diversification. Evidence: https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/05/oecd-economic-surveys-new-zealand-2026_27daa8d8/full-report/unlocking-capital-markets-to-drive-growth_d1f7a7f7.html

p6-c4-b1.label: High-value employment expanded
p6-c4-b1.detailText: Manufacturing employs more than 220,000 people and employment indicators have recently improved, but this sits against a long decline in the sector's share of the economy. Evidence: https://stats.govt.nz/topics/manufacturing-and-production

p6-c4-b2.label: Manufacturing base broadened
p6-c4-b2.detailText: The base has narrowed, not broadened. Manufacturing's share of real GDP has fallen from around 15 percent in 1990 to about 8 percent, with non-food manufacturing essentially flat for three decades. Evidence: https://stats.govt.nz/topics/manufacturing-and-production

p6-c5-b0.label: Reliance on narrow primary exports reduced
p6-c5-b0.detailText: Reliance has increased rather than reduced. Dairy alone is around 30 percent of exports, food and fibre is at a record $64.3 billion, and Treasury has documented rising export concentration. Evidence: https://www.treasury.govt.nz/publications/research-and-commentary/rangitaki-blog/mei-special-topic-new-zealands-increasing-export-concentration

savedState.boardInfo:
Proof-of-concept DoView Board modelling the argument in Sean Doherty's article "New Zealand's favourite economies do not succeed by accident" (NZ Manufacturer, 19 August 2026). The board sets out what would have to happen, and in what order, for the focused industrial policy the article calls for to produce the productivity, export and wage outcomes it points to in Singapore, Ireland and Denmark.

This is a model of one commentator's argument. It is not government policy, not an agreed plan, and not endorsed by the author, NZ Manufacturer, or any agency. The causal links express the article's reasoning and several are genuinely contestable — that is the point of putting them on a board where they can be seen and argued with.

Built with the official DoView Boards V1.4.3 prompt package. This work uses the DoView Planning approach and DoView Boards developed by Dr Paul Duignan. See DoViewPlanning.org.

TRAFFIC LIGHTS ON THIS BOARD ARE AN AI ASSESSMENT. Each This-Then box carries a traffic light rating how well New Zealand appears to be doing on that outcome, with the reasoning and a supporting public source in the box Display Text. These ratings were generated by an AI system reading public evidence in August 2026. They are a starting point for argument, not an authoritative scorecard, and they have not been reviewed by the article's author, by any agency, or by any domain expert. Where public evidence did not support a judgement, the box is left grey rather than guessed at.

pageInfo.p1: Follows the article's central claim: New Zealand cites Singapore, Ireland and Denmark as benchmarks but has not adopted the focused industrial policy behind their results. The page treats the political argument as a real causal stage, not a preamble.
pageInfo.p2: A supply pipeline whose real bottleneck sits late, inside firms, rather than at the training end. Density is therefore loaded on the fourth column, where trained people either land, reskill and stay, or do not.
pageInfo.p3: A barrier-removal page: each diagnosed barrier is answered by a matched support instrument, then narrows to firm behaviour and its productivity consequence. Wide at the front, narrow at the back, because many barriers converge on one investment decision.
pageInfo.p4: The shortest page, and deliberately so. Denmark's Red Carpet reasoning is a gate rather than a chain: constraints are either cleared or the project goes offshore. Three stages capture it without inventing intermediate outcomes.
pageInfo.p5: A translation chain from research direction to retained value, addressing the article's point about too little commercialisation. Density peaks in the second column because connection mechanisms, not research volume, are where the chain breaks.
pageInfo.p6: The longest page because scaling is genuinely the longest journey in the article: capital alone is insufficient, so a capability column sits between finance and market entry, and the export-mix shift is a separate later consequence rather than a restatement of scale.
pageInfo.p7: Level 1 delivery workstreams implied by the article's list of things comparator countries actually backed. Illustrative only — a real board would replace these with named programmes and owners.
pageInfo.p8: Level 2 functions rather than named agencies, because the article argues about policy design rather than machinery of government. Replace with the actual organisations before operational use.
pageInfo.p9: A no-level page for cross-cutting competencies. Competencies are mapped selectively to Level 1 workstreams in Step 2; several may carry no links at all.
pageInfo.overview: Six pathways drawn from the article, plus How Pages for workstreams, functions and competencies. Start with Policy direction and mandate — the article's argument is that nothing downstream happens without it.
pageInfo.final: The outcomes the article points to when it cites Singapore, Ireland and Denmark. The last one is the article's closing warning stated positively.

docContent.p10:
Purpose

This board is a proof-of-concept DoView model of the argument set out by Sean Doherty in New Zealand's favourite economies do not succeed by accident, published by NZ Manufacturer on 19 August 2026. It turns that opinion piece into an explicit outcomes model so the causal claims inside it can be seen, tested and argued with.

Scope

The board covers six pathways drawn from the article: policy direction and mandate; skills and workforce capability; technology adoption and firm productivity; industrial land, energy and consenting; applied research and commercialisation; and capital, scaling and export growth. It does not cover fiscal settings, tax design, immigration policy beyond specialist skills, trade agreements, or the machinery-of-government questions the article does not raise.

Assumptions

  • The article's core claim is treated as the board's spine: that comparator-country performance follows deliberate policy choices rather than accident.
  • Level 2 How Boxes name functions rather than specific agencies, because the article argues about policy design, not institutional structure.
  • Comparator detail is used as the article reports it. No additional claims about Singapore, Ireland or Denmark have been added from other sources.
  • Causal direction reflects the article's reasoning, not independently established evidence. Several links are contestable and are meant to be argued about.

Sources

The board content derives from a single public source, listed in board Sources: Sean Doherty, "New Zealand's favourite economies do not succeed by accident", NZ Manufacturer, 19 August 2026 — nzmanufacturer.co.nz. Quotations attributed in that article to Gan Kim Yong, Peter Burke and Morten Bødskov are not reproduced here; box labels paraphrase the article's argument in outcome form.

Traffic light assessments

Every This–Then box carries a traffic light recording an assessment of how well New Zealand is currently doing on that outcome, with the reasoning and a supporting public source in the box Display Text. Green indicates the outcome is largely being achieved; red indicates it is not; grey means public evidence did not support a judgement either way.

These ratings are an AI assessment made in August 2026 from public sources. They are intended to provoke argument, not to settle it. They have not been reviewed by the article's author, by NZ Manufacturer, by any agency, or by any domain expert. Several ratings turn on judgement calls a specialist would reasonably contest — particularly on the policy and mandate page, where the assessment tracks the article's own argument closely. Check each rating against its source before relying on it.

Cautions and limitations

  • This is a model of one commentator's argument, not a government strategy, an agreed plan, or an evidence review.
  • The board is AI-assisted and has not been reviewed by the author, by NZ Manufacturer, or by any agency.
  • Boxes are illustrative outcome statements. Measures and evaluation questions are placeholders for discussion, not a monitoring framework.
  • Uncertainty is highest on the cross-page links, where one pathway is assumed to enable another.

Attribution

This work uses the DoView Planning approach and DoView Boards developed by Dr Paul Duignan. See DoViewPlanning.org.

The underlying argument is the work of Sean Doherty, Manufacturing Commentator, NZ Industry Trends, published in NZ Manufacturer. Modelling it here does not imply his endorsement, or NZ Manufacturer's, of this board or of any interpretation in it.
docContent.p11:
Illustrative monitoring and evaluation plan

This is a placeholder plan, not a monitoring framework. It shows the shape a monitoring and evaluation plan would take for a board like this one. Every measure, question, baseline, target, owner and reporting cycle would need to be established by the people accountable for the work before any of it is used.

What would be monitored

The board's measures sit against the outcomes where movement would be observable earliest. They are deliberately few.

What would be evaluated

Monitoring shows movement; it does not explain it. These questions are the ones a real evaluation would need to answer, and they are the ones most likely to be uncomfortable.

Sequencing

  • Early. Whether the policy direction actually held, and whether sector choices were made transparently. Governance evidence, not outcome data.
  • Middle. Whether support instruments reached the firms they were designed for, particularly smaller ones, and whether skills provision shifted.
  • Late. Whether productivity, scaling and export composition moved. These lag by years and are heavily influenced by factors outside the board.

Attribution caution

Productivity and export-mix outcomes have many causes. Exchange rates, commodity cycles, global demand and firm-level decisions will move these numbers regardless of policy. Any evaluation should treat contribution rather than attribution as the realistic standard, and should say plainly where it cannot separate policy effect from context.

Known gaps in this placeholder

No baselines, no targets, no data sources, no owners, no reporting cycle, no cost information, and no evaluation design. A real plan needs all of these.

Using DoView Boards and Disclaimer

See the disclaimer section below.

The DoView Board prompt and the DoView Board built within this DoView Board prototype app are provided free of charge so that anyone can experiment with DoView Boards and explore for themselves how they can answer the 20 key questions that anyone running or overseeing an organization needs to answer. See https://doviewplanning.org/doviewboards.

Walk-Through

To get a walk-through for using DoView Boards, see https://doviewplanning.org/walkthrough.

Accessing Consulting or Training

We can provide consulting or training on integrating the use of DoView Boards into your existing planning, implementation and reporting workflows in business, government, or nonprofit settings. See https://doviewplanning.org/offerings.

Adapting the DoView Board Prototype App to your setting

This DoView Board is being used within the DoView Board prototype app. It is a free of charge app that runs inside any browser window and can be used for piloting, testing, proof-of-concept and for use where confidential information is not being included and where there is a low security risk.

Because it is an open-source project, any developer can extend, harden, adapt, or include features of the DoView Board app in other planning products or systems to suit specific deployment requirements. Use entirely at your own risk.
